title: The mountains remain
hookLine: Du Fu in wartime: the nation is broken, mountains and rivers remain (Spring View, 757)
tomorrow: an empty mountain, voices, no one in sight. where's the light?

cards: Some weeks the news makes it feel like everything is breaking at once. Du Fu lived through that. A rebellion has taken the capital, and he's stuck inside the captured city, his family far away.
He writes: the nation is broken; mountains and rivers remain. Spring comes to the city anyway, and the grass and trees grow deep.

teach.b: The poem doesn't stay calm. Feeling the times, he says, even flowers draw tears; hating the parting, even birds startle the heart. A letter from home is worth ten thousand in gold.
His white hair is so thin it can barely hold a hairpin.
Notice the order: he names the break first. Only then does he look for what's still standing. You've met that first line on this path already: it's the one Basho remembered, weeping, at Hiraizumi.

Tradition calls Du Fu the poet-sage, and the sage he stands nearest is Confucius, who said, in Legge's English: "When the year becomes cold, then we know how the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves."
Under the mountains sits a Confucian teaching: goodness is proved by steadiness when things fall apart, the evergreen in the cold.
Du Fu doesn't pretend the nation is fine, and he doesn't pretend the hills are gone.

how: Readers return to Du Fu's Spring View in hard times. Confucian teaching holds up the pine and cypress, green in winter, as the picture of steady goodness.

o: a farmers' rule to build their houses on high ground
Du Fu's line: the nation broken, the hills still standing
a saying that mountains outlast every emperor's name

p: still there when the nation breaks

s: Du Fu's poem says the war didn't matter because nature goes on
he names the break first and grieves; even his hair is thinning.
Confucius said the cold year shows the pine and cypress
the Analects: they're the last to lose their leaves.
in the poem, a letter from home is worth ten thousand in gold
his family was far away, beyond the fighting.

games.q: a friend's family shop just closed. he says "everything's ruined." what fits Du Fu?
o: it's broken, and that's real. what's still standing?
look on the bright side; it wasn't that important.
nothing lasts anyway, so there's no point grieving.
games.why: Du Fu names the break first: the nation is broken. only then: mountains and rivers remain.

practice: Count what remains. On your fingers, one at a time, name something still standing in your life this week: a person, a place, a habit, a body that breathes. Don't skip the hard things; let the count sit beside them.

wordCard.voice: The mountains remain: Du Fu's broken city, and the hills still standing around it.

orig.note: Chinese: the nation is broken; mountains and rivers remain. The first line of Du Fu's Spring View.

carryVoice: Carry this one: the mountains remain, so name the break, then find the pine. One week of poets, done.

sources.q: 國破山河在，城春草木深。
